ExRL: Sample-Efficient Online Adaptation of
Long-Chunk Policies via Execution Length Control

Xu Luo1, Jiaying Yang2, Hao Wu1, Junlin Xie1, Zijin Hong3, Ji Zhang1, Lianli Gao1, Jingkuan Song2 Affiliation: 1UESTC 2Tongji University 3The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
\sublargesizehttps://exrl-project.github.io
Abstract

Predicting long action chunks, often spanning dozens of timesteps, has become a key ingredient in increasingly capable robot policies. In this paper, we find that adapting these long-chunk policies with existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods can require many online samples due to the high dimensionality of the action chunks being optimized, making such adaptation impractical in real-world scenarios where interaction data are costly to collect. Our key insight is to shift adaptation from optimizing actions to optimizing how long to execute each predicted action chunk. This keeps the adaptation space low-dimensional while its expressivity grows with the chunk size. We thus introduce Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), a simple approach which augments the base policy with a lightweight adapter that predicts the execution length of each chunk and is trained using off-policy RL algorithms. Across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks, ExRL enables sample-efficient adaptation of a diverse range of long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific hyperparameter tuning.

††aftertitle: Fig. 1: We propose ExRL, a sample-efficient RL method for adapting long-chunk policies through execution-length control. Left: Existing RL methods lose sample efficiency as action chunks grow longer, while ExRL maintains high learning efficiency. Right: ExRL improves π0.5\pi_{0.5} policies to high success rates on contact-rich and long-horizon real-world tasks with only tens of minutes of physical interaction or a few hundred episodes.

I Introduction

Robot policies trained on demonstration datasets have enabled increasingly complex and generalizable behaviors across a wide range of robotic control tasks [57, 1]. A key technique shared by many of these policies is action chunking [70]. Rather than predicting a single action at each query, action-chunked policies predict a sequence of actions and execute them open-loop, which can help capture non-Markovian structure in demonstrations [32, 39] and reduce compounding errors [32, 68]. A common choice in recent robot policies is to predict long action chunks, often exceeding 20 steps and approaching 50, as in vision-language-action (VLA) models such as π0.5\pi_{0.5} [8] and π0\pi_{0}-FAST [48], and world action models such as DreamZero [65]. By producing many actions per model query, long chunks enable high-frequency control (e.g., 50 Hz) for dexterous tasks such as laundry folding [9], while reducing inference pauses for smoother, faster execution.

These long-chunk robot policies, while performant, are rarely optimal when deployed in the real world due to limited demonstration coverage and imperfect generalization [55]. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a direct way to adapt these policies from online experience. In other domains such as language modeling, online RL has been shown to be quite effective for adapting models pretrained on offline datasets [45, 24, 21]. For robotic control, however, online data collection in the real world is often slow, costly, and sometimes unsafe, making sample efficiency a central requirement.

Yet we observe that long action chunks introduce a major bottleneck for sample-efficient adaptation (Figure , left). RL methods that optimize entire action chunks or their latent variables face an increasingly high-dimensional optimization space as the chunk length grows. This substantially increases the amount of online experience required for adaptation.

This motivates us to seek an adaptation interface whose dimensionality does not grow with the chunk length. We observe that action-chunked policies naturally expose such an interface, namely, how long to execute a predicted chunk before querying the policy again. Although execution length is a simple scalar decision, adapting it to the current state and predicted action chunk can substantially alter policy behavior by controlling the trade-off between longer open-loop execution, which better exploits the benefits of action chunking, and shorter execution, which improves responsiveness to unexpected state changes or dynamics mismatch [39]. This makes execution length a meaningful variable for policy improvement, while being particularly attractive for long chunks: as the chunk size grows, the number of possible execution lengths—and hence the expressivity—increases, whereas the optimization itself remains a low-dimensional discrete problem.

We instantiate this idea as Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), a sample-efficient online RL method for adapting long-chunk policies. It adds a lightweight execution-length policy that selects how many actions from each predicted chunk to execute before replanning, and trains it using standard off-policy RL algorithms. Because this adapter can be learned without modifying the base policy itself, ExRL provides a policy-agnostic interface that can be applied to virtually any class of action-chunked policies. Execution-length control is ultimately bounded by the capabilities of the underlying base policy. To go beyond this limitation, we can further optionally distill successful online trajectories back into the base policy during RL using simple imitation loss, allowing the base policy itself to improve alongside the adapter. Finally, ExRL can also leverage general offline data, such as human demonstrations, by reinterpreting arbitrary trajectory segments as off-policy experience under different execution lengths, further improving online sample efficiency.

We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of ExRL across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, showing state-of-the-art online adaptation performance across a range of long-chunk policies, largely without task-specific hyperparameter tuning. These include standard action-chunked policies, different classes of pretrained VLA models such as π0.5\pi_{0.5} [8] and π0\pi_{0}-FAST [48], as well as a world action model, Cosmos Policy [27]. On real-world tasks spanning precise manipulation, long-horizon coordination, and clothing folding, ExRL efficiently adapts frozen π0.5\pi_{0.5} policies, approaching perfect success on cube stacking with about ten minutes of physical interaction.

II Related Work

Imitation learning in robotics. Imitation learning, particularly behavior cloning, has been widely used to train data-driven policies for robotic control [5, 51, 69, 18, 52]. Prior work has explored a wide range of action parameterizations and policy architectures for imitation learning. Earlier methods often represent actions with Gaussian or GMM policies [25, 41], while more recent approaches use expressive generative modeling techniques, including VAEs [70], diffusion or flow models [14, 44, 9, 7], and autoregressive next-token prediction models [72, 28, 48]. With the growing scale of human demonstration datasets and policy models [60, 26, 11, 46], imitation learning has further become a pretraining paradigm for generalist robot policies, absorbing broad prior knowledge into a single model that can be adapted for real-world deployment [44, 28, 9]. Our work provides an efficient method to adapt these diverse policy classes from online experience.

Adaptive execution of action chunks. Action chunking, as used in ACT [70], has become a de facto design choice in robot policies learned with imitation learning. Recognizing that the execution length of action chunks strongly affects policy behavior [54, 68, 39], several concurrent works have explored adaptive execution strategies. Earlier RL methods such as Dynamic Action Repetition [31] and TempoRL [6] adapt how long a primitive action is repeated, rather than how much of a predicted action chunk is executed. AAC [36] selects the execution length of vision-language-action models using action entropy, while FFDC [61] selects the execution length for world action models using a learned verifier to check whether predicted future observations remain consistent with the real rollout. ExRL instead learns execution-length decisions directly from task rewards through online RL. TAS [63] uses online RL to select among actions cached from overlapping chunks at every timestep, rather than explicitly learning a chunk-level execution length. Two other recent works, ACSAC [13] and ACH [53], learn value-based adaptive chunk-size selection for offline-to-online RL. However, these methods train and evaluate specific chunked policies within offline and offline-to-online RL frameworks, and are not designed as plug-in adapters for arbitrary pretrained action-chunked policies. The closest work to ours is [71], a concurrent study that also adapts action-chunked policies through reinforcement learning over execution length. However, it relies on PPO for optimization; our comparison in Appendix B shows that off-policy learning can adapt execution lengths with substantially fewer online samples.

Reinforcement learning for robot policy adaptation. On-policy methods such as PPO and GRPO have been used to fine-tune pretrained robot policies [34, 40, 12, 50], but often require many online rollouts, limiting their practicality on real robots. Off-policy RL algorithms such as SAC [22] and TD3 [20] can use data more efficiently, but their standard implementations typically use deterministic or Gaussian actors, making direct adaptation of more complex generative policies nontrivial. Policy-specific approaches address this challenge in different ways: DSRL [59] and ZPRL [66] optimize diffusion/flow policies in latent spaces. OGPO [47] uses off-policy critics to guide optimization of the diffusion or flow generation process, while RL-100 [33] applies PPO-style updates across diffusion denoising steps. These methods can improve sample efficiency, but remain tied to particular policy classes. Residual RL instead learns additive corrections to the base actions [67, 4, 3, 16, 56]. While policy-agnostic and lightweight, residual RL still requires continuous action optimization; correcting an entire chunk makes this space grow with chunk length. RL Token [64] learns a lightweight actor conditioned on VLA representations and reference chunks, with regularization toward the base actions. PA-RL [42] achieves policy-agnostic adaptation by casting RL as action optimization followed by supervised policy learning. RECAP [2] builds an offline-to-online pipeline for training advantage-conditioned policies, which can incorporate batch online RL [17] for efficient adaptation. In contrast to these action-modifying approaches, ExRL adapts the execution length of each predicted chunk, reducing online adaptation to a compact discrete decision space and enabling sample-efficient, policy-agnostic adaptation.

III Preliminaries

Markov decision processes. Markov decision process (MDP) is denoted by a tuple ℳ=(𝒮,𝒜,P,r,ρ0,γ)\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r,\rho_{0},\gamma), where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the state space, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the action space, P(⋅∣s,a)P(\cdot\mid s,a) is the transition dynamics, r:𝒮×𝒜→ℝr:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is the reward function, ρ0\rho_{0} is the initial state distribution, and γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1) is the discount factor. A policy π:𝒮→Δ⁡(𝒜)\pi:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\Delta(\mathcal{A}) is a mapping from states to distributions over actions. The QQ-function, or critic, of a policy π\pi is defined as Qπ(s,a)=𝔼π[∑t≥0γtr(st,at)∣s0=s,a0=a]Q^{\pi}(s,a)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\sum_{t\geq 0}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\mid s_{0}=s,a_{0}=a], which is the expected discounted return of π\pi from taking action aa in state ss. The goal of reinforcement learning is to find a policy that maximizes the expected discounted return.

Q-learning. A broad class of RL algorithms learns a parameterized Q-function Qϕ​(st,at)Q_{\phi}(s_{t},a_{t}) by bootstrapping from Bellman targets. Given a transition (st,at,rt,st+1)(s_{t},a_{t},r_{t},s_{t+1}), a generic one-step temporal-difference (TD) target takes the form

yt=rt+γ​V​(st+1),y_{t}=r_{t}+\gamma V(s_{t+1}), (1)

where VV denotes the bootstrap value of the next decision state induced by the particular algorithm. The critic is then trained by minimizing the squared TD error

minϕ⁡𝔼⁡[(Qϕ​(st,at)−yt)2].\min_{\phi}\;\mathbb{E}\left[\left(Q_{\phi}(s_{t},a_{t})-y_{t}\right)^{2}\right]. (2)

Action chunking. An action-chunked policy π\pi is a mapping 𝒮→Δ⁡(𝒜H)\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\Delta(\mathcal{A}^{H}) from states to distributions over HH-step action sequences. At a query state sts_{t}, a standard action-chunked policy samples an action chunk at:t+H=[at,at+1,…,at+H−1]∼π(⋅∣st)a_{t:t+H}=[a_{t},a_{t+1},...,a_{t+H-1}]\sim\pi(\ \cdot\mid s_{t}), and then executes at:t+ka_{t:t+k}, where 1≤k≤H1\leq k\leq H is a fixed execution length, after which the policy is queried again at state st+ks_{t+k}.

Problem setting. In this paper, we assume access to a pretrained action-chunked policy πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}}, and our goal is to adapt it to maximize the expected return specified by some reward rr using online interactions with an environment ℳ\mathcal{M}. Note that we make no assumptions on the parameterization or architecture of πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}}.

IV Execution at the Right Length

We propose ExRL, which adapts action-chunked policies by dynamically controlling how long each predicted action chunk is executed before replanning, rather than modifying the action chunk itself (Figure 2). In this section, we formalize this idea as reinforcement learning over execution-length decisions.

Given a pretrained action-chunked policy πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} with chunk size HH, we learn an additional execution-length policy πex:𝒮×𝒜H→Δ⁡(𝒦)\pi_{\mathrm{ex}}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}^{H}\rightarrow\Delta(\mathcal{K}), where 𝒦={1,…,H}\mathcal{K}=\{1,\ldots,H\}. At each query, πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} first predicts an action chunk, and πex\pi_{\mathrm{ex}} maps the current state and this predicted chunk to a distribution over feasible execution lengths. In this way, the raw primitive actions are still produced by πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}}, while the learned execution-length policy acts in the much smaller discrete space 𝒦\mathcal{K}, avoiding direct optimization in the continuous, high-dimensional space of action chunks. We can also optionally allow the policy to choose k=0k=0, corresponding to executing none of the actions in the current chunk, which is essentially an immediate replanning decision.

Duration-aware Q-learning. The execution-length decision naturally leads to a temporally extended Q-function. At a query timestep tt, let at:t+Ha_{t:t+H} denote the action chunk sampled from πbase(⋅∣st)\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(\ \cdot\mid s_{t}). In ExRL, we learn a critic Qϕ(st,at:t+H,k)Q_{\phi}(s_{t},a_{t:t+H},k), which estimates the return obtained by executing the first kk actions of the predicted chunk and then continuing with the current execution-length strategy. This is closely related to Q-chunking [35], which learns a critic over an action sequence rather than a single primitive action. The difference is that in Q-chunking, the critic evaluates the action chunks, while the critic in ExRL evaluates the selected prefix lengths of action chunks. Thus, the accumulated reward and the bootstrap discount in ExRL both depend on the chosen “meta-action” ktk_{t}, leading to the duration-aware TD target below:

yt=∑i=0kt−1γi​r​(st+i,at+i)+γkt​V​(s′,a′),y_{t}=\sum_{i=0}^{k_{t}-1}\gamma^{i}r(s_{t+i},a_{t+i})+\gamma^{k_{t}}V(s^{\prime},a^{\prime}), (3)

where s′=st+kts^{\prime}=s_{t+k_{t}} is the next query state, a′=at+kt:t+kt+H∼πbase(⋅∣s′)a^{\prime}=a_{t+k_{t}:t+k_{t}+H}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(\ \cdot\,\mid s^{\prime}) is the next chunk sampled from the frozen base policy, and VV is the next-state value. This duration-aware backup mirrors the Bellman backup used in semi-Markov decision processes (SMDPs) [58], where temporally extended decisions may last for a variable number of primitive timesteps. In Appendix E, we formalize this connection by showing how execution-length control induces an SMDP under the frozen base policy πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}}.

Practical instantiations. ExRL is agnostic to the choice of RL algorithm, as long as the algorithm can optimize over the discrete execution-length space with the duration-aware backup above. In practice, we instantiate ExRL with two off-policy variants for sample-efficient online adaptation. The first variant, ExRL-Q, utilizes the discrete nature of the action space and uses value-based RL without learning an explicit actor [62, 43]. In this case, the next-state value VV is computed by a Bellman optimality backup:

V⁡(s′,a′)=maxk′∈𝒦⁡Qϕ¯​(s′,a′,k′),V(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})=\max_{k^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}}Q_{\bar{\phi}}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime},k^{\prime}), (4)

where Qϕ¯Q_{\bar{\phi}} is a slowly-updated target, and the critic is trained by minimizing the squared TD error:

ℒQ(ϕ)=𝔼[(Qϕ(st,at:t+H,kt)−yt)2].\mathcal{L}_{Q}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(Q_{\phi}(s_{t},a_{t:t+H},k_{t})-y_{t}\right)^{2}\right]. (5)

During online rollout, the execution length is selected greedily as

kt=arg​maxk∈𝒦Qϕ(st,at:t+H,k).k_{t}=\argmax_{k\in\mathcal{K}}Q_{\phi}(s_{t},a_{t:t+H},k). (6)

The second variant, ExRL-SAC, adds an explicit actor πψ(kt∣st,at:t+H)\pi_{\psi}(k_{t}\mid s_{t},a_{t:t+H}) that outputs a categorical distribution over execution lengths. Since 𝒦\mathcal{K} is discrete, we use discrete SAC [15] as an actor-critic instantiation. Compared with continuous-action SAC, the discrete action space allows us to compute the policy value exactly by summing over all k∈𝒦k\in\mathcal{K}. In this case, the hard maximum in ExRL-Q is replaced by the soft value under the actor. The soft value is

V⁡(s′,a′)=\displaystyle V(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})={} ∑k′∈𝒦πψ(k′∣s′,a′)[Qϕ¯(s′,a′,k′)\displaystyle\sum_{k^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}}\pi_{\psi}(k^{\prime}\mid s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\bigl[Q_{\bar{\phi}}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime},k^{\prime}) (7)
−αlogπψ(k′∣s′,a′)].\displaystyle-\alpha\log\pi_{\psi}(k^{\prime}\mid s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\bigr].

The entropy term −α​log⁡πψ-\alpha\log\pi_{\psi} encourages the policy to maintain uncertainty over execution lengths, which improves exploration and prevents early collapse to a single fixed kk. Squared TD error is used to update the critic, and the actor is trained to choose execution length with high soft value:

ℒπ​(ψ)=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\pi}(\psi)={} −𝔼kt∼πψ(⋅∣st,at:t+H)[Qϕ(st,at:t+H,kt)\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}_{k_{t}\sim\pi_{\psi}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t:t+H})}\bigl[Q_{\phi}(s_{t},a_{t:t+H},k_{t}) (8)
−αlogπψ(kt∣st,at:t+H)].\displaystyle-\alpha\log\pi_{\psi}(k_{t}\mid s_{t},a_{t:t+H})\bigr].

Both ExRL-Q and ExRL-SAC further use conservative Q-learning (CQL) [30] to reduce overestimation of execution lengths with limited support in the replay data. Specifically, we augment the TD objective with

ℒcritic(ϕ)=ℒQ(ϕ)+λCQL𝔼(s,a,k)∼𝒟[log(1|𝒦|∑k′∈𝒦expQϕ(s,a,k′))−Qϕ(s,a,k)],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{critic}}(\phi)=\mathcal{L}_{Q}(\phi)+\lambda_{\mathrm{CQL}}\mathbb{E}_{(s,a,k)\sim\mathcal{D}}\Biggl[\\ \log\biggl(\frac{1}{|\mathcal{K}|}\sum_{k^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}}\exp Q_{\phi}(s,a,k^{\prime})\biggr)-Q_{\phi}(s,a,k)\Biggr], (9)

where 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the replay buffer and λCQL\lambda_{\mathrm{CQL}} controls the regularization strength. The algorithms of ExRL-Q and ExRL-SAC are summarized in Algorithm 1 and 2, respectively.

ExRL + online behavior cloning (BC). ExRL can improve policies without changing the actions proposed within each chunk, but its capability is ultimately bounded by the underlying base policy. How can we go beyond this limitation? We note that, by replanning at adaptive times, ExRL can stitch together prefixes from different predicted chunks and produce successful trajectories that would not arise from simply executing the original long chunks open-loop. We can therefore distill these improved behaviors back into the base policy during RL (Figure 2). Specifically, from each successful ExRL rollout, we construct HH-step action-chunk targets from the primitive actions actually executed, even when a target spans multiple replanning decisions, and update πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} using the same behavior cloning objective as in pretraining. In this way, behaviors discovered through execution-length adaptation become direct supervision for the base policy, improving its chunk predictions and in turn providing a stronger basis for further adaptation.

Leveraging offline data. ExRL can also reuse general offline trajectories, such as human demonstrations, even if they were collected without action chunking. The key observation is that any sequence of recorded primitive actions can be retrospectively treated as a virtual action chunk (Figure 3). Its prefixes of different lengths then provide real experience of executing the same action sequence for different lengths. Concretely, before online training, we enumerate trajectory segments of all lengths k≤Hk\leq H from offline trajectories and add the corresponding execution-length transitions to the replay buffer. For each transition, the offline trajectory provides the accumulated rewards and resulting state for the executed prefix; from that state onward, the value target bootstraps with the current base policy and execution-length strategy. This anchors the value of each virtual chunk to the expected return under ExRL’s actual execution strategy, rather than to the behavior that generated the offline trajectory. When online behavior cloning is enabled, demonstration data can also be mixed with successful online trajectories to jointly update the base policy.

Remark. One may ask why we do not simply use a short fixed execution length for previous RL methods to avoid high-dimensional optimization, or first select the optimal fixed execution length and then optimize on top of it. Always using a short execution length for RL, however, can be problematic for several reasons: it may yield very poor initial performance on some tasks, making RL optimization difficult; it requires more frequent policy queries, increasing training cost and inference overhead while potentially introducing inference–execution synchronization issues; and, on long-horizon tasks, it substantially increases the effective decision horizon, further complicating RL. Alternatively, preselecting an optimal fixed execution length instead requires extensive real-world evaluation, potentially hundreds of rollouts, which is already comparable to the interaction budget of a typical real-world online RL experiment.

V Experiments

The goal of our experiments is to answer the following core questions:

  1. (Q1)

    Can ExRL enable sample-efficient adaptation across action-chunked policies, including generalist robot policies in both simulation and real-world tasks?

  2. (Q2)

    Can updating the base policy with successful online trajectories and demonstrations further improve adaptation?

  3. (Q3)

    What execution-length patterns does ExRL learn?

V-A Base Policies

To show the generality of our method, we conduct experiments on diverse classes of action-chunked policies. We consider both representative action-chunked policies trained with imitation learning and several pretrained generalist robot policies of different classes.

Representative action-chunked policies: (1) Diffusion Policy (DP) [14]: an action-chunked policy that models multimodal continuous action chunks using denoising diffusion [23]; and (2) ACT [70]: a transformer-based policy that predicts action chunks using an encoder–decoder architecture.

Generalist robot policies. (1) π0\pi_{0} [9] and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [8]: state-of-the-art VLA models that use flow matching [37] to model action chunks; (2) π0\pi_{0}-FAST [48]: an autoregressive VLA model that generates action chunks through efficient action tokenization; and (3) Cosmos Policy [27]: a world action model built on a large pretrained video generation model.

V-B Baselines and Setup

We compare ExRL against execution-length baselines and several online adaptation baselines, with a focus on policy-agnostic methods for action-chunked policies. Our baselines include:

Execution-length baselines. (1) Random-kk: randomly samples an execution length from the feasible set at each policy query; (2) Optimal fixed-kk: sweeps fixed execution lengths and reports the best-performing one.
AAC [36]: A training-free adaptive execution method that selects the execution length using action entropy.
Online BC: An ablation that directly distills successful online rollouts back into the base policy using behavior cloning without RL.
Policy Decorator [67]: An off-policy residual RL method that freezes the base policy and learns additive corrections to its predicted actions, with bounded residuals and controlled exploration for stable online learning.
DSRL [59]: A latent steering method for diffusion- and flow-based policies that keeps the base policy frozen and applies RL in its initial latent-noise space rather than directly modifying the generated actions.
PA-RL [42]: A policy-agnostic RL finetuning method that uses a learned critic to improve action candidates through re-ranking and local optimization, and then distills the improved actions back into the base policy.
OGPO [47]: An off-policy full-finetuning method for diffusion- and flow-based policies. It learns off-policy critics for data reuse and uses their values to optimize the full diffusion or flow generation process through a modified PPO objective.
ResFiT [3]: A demo-augmented residual RL method that keeps the base policy frozen, constrains residual magnitude for stable exploration, and jointly trains on demonstration and online data; we adapt its original per-step residual formulation to operate over action chunks.
DICE-RL [56]: Also a demo-augmented residual RL method that combines value-guided action selection with selective behavior regularization to reinforce high-value behaviors while remaining close to the pretrained policy.

Simulation benchmarks and setup. We consider three simulation benchmarks: Robomimic [41], spanning five tabletop manipulation tasks from simple tasks to challenging long-horizon tasks such as Tool Hang and Transport; Adroit [49], spanning four high-frequency dexterous hand manipulation tasks (H=32H=32); and a LIBERO [38] task following the DSRL setup, except that we use H=50H=50 instead of H=10H=10. On Robomimic, the main experiments use H=50H=50 for DP and ACT; Appendix Figure 13 reports additional H=32H=32 results for both policies. Following prior work [59, 47], we use base-policy checkpoints that leave meaningful headroom for RL improvement. Our goal on these benchmarks is not to maximize base-policy performance, but to use them as a controlled testbed for evaluating long-chunk policy adaptation. For each variant of ExRL, we keep most hyperparameters fixed across tasks and make only a few task-level adjustments when necessary, such as the discount factor γ\gamma and network width. Appendix A provides task details, policy architectures, baseline adaptations, and hyperparameter settings. For each run in the plot, we report the average success rate and 95% confidence intervals over three seeds.

V-C Sample-Efficient Adaptation in Simulation

Figures 5, 5, and 8 show that ExRL substantially improves frozen base policies, often reaching success rates close to 100%100\% by learning only the execution length. The gains over the optimal fixed-kk baseline are particularly large on DP Can, Square, and Tool Hang, and across all four LIBERO policies. As these improvements require no changes to the actions predicted by the base policy, they validate the importance and expressiveness of execution-length control as an adaptation interface.

Compared with other RL methods, ExRL often learns substantially faster, particularly early in online adaptation. On LIBERO, for example, it improves π0.5\pi_{0.5} from nearly 0%0\% to over 90%90\% success within 200,000200{,}000 environment steps. The advantage is also pronounced on the challenging Tool Hang task, where ExRL-SAC achieves high success with both DP and ACT; with DP, it exceeds 90%90\% success while all other baselines remain at around 20%20\% or below.

Online BC further improves both sample efficiency and final performance, particularly on DP Transport and several Adroit tasks. In these settings, ExRL-Q + Online BC substantially outperforms both frozen-base ExRL-Q and Online BC alone, supporting the value of distilling the improved behaviors discovered by ExRL back into the base policy.

With demonstration augmentation, ExRL-Q + Online BC rapidly reaches near-perfect success on ACT Can and all four Adroit tasks, competitive with the strongest demonstration-based baselines.

Figure 7 further isolates the benefit of demonstrations for execution-length learning: adding human experience to RL replay accelerates early adaptation on Can while keeping the base policy frozen.

The LIBERO results also highlight the generality of ExRL. The same execution-length formulation enables efficient adaptation of flow-based VLAs, autoregressive VLAs, and a world action model, despite their substantially different architectures and action-generation processes.

V-D Sample-Efficient Real-World Adaptation

We further adapt π0.5\pi_{0.5} with chunk size H=50H=50 on four real-world tasks (Figure , right; Table I). Power insertion requires contact-rich manipulation, while clothing folding involves manipulating deformable objects. Both clothing folding and parts organization require long-horizon coordination. We report success rate for stacking, folding, and insertion, and the fraction of completed stages for organization. Further setup details are provided in Appendix A-G.

The sample efficiency of ExRL carries over to real-world adaptation. With the base policy frozen, ExRL-Q approaches 100%100\% success on stack cube with only ten minutes of physical interaction, and reaches nearly 90%90\% on the long-horizon clothing folding task within 8585 minutes. Power insertion and parts organization similarly improve within a few hundred rollouts. Final evaluations show substantial gains over fixed-length execution across all four tasks (Table I).

V-E Ablation Studies

Accounting for the selected execution length in reward accumulation and discounting improves learning over a TD target that treats each decision as a single step (Figure 8, leftmost panel). The predicted chunk is also essential to the decision: conditioning on both the observation and the chunk raises success from around 30%30\% to nearly 90%90\% compared with observations alone (second panel). Thus, the critic benefits from knowing what the base policy proposes, beyond the current state. Allowing k=0k=0 offers little additional benefit over positive execution lengths (third panel), while similar learning curves across network widths from 128128 to 20482048 suggest that ExRL does not require precise tuning of network capacity (rightmost panel).

V-F What Execution Length Patterns Does ExRL Learn?

ExRL improves a policy without changing its predicted actions, raising the question of how execution-length decisions reshape its behavior. Figure 9(a) reveals a consistent pattern: across Lift, Can, Square, and real-world insertion, ExRL selects shorter executions near the object or target than during free motion. The mean length roughly halves in simulation and falls to about a quarter on real-world insertion. ExRL therefore concentrates replanning near interaction, while allowing longer motions elsewhere.

Short executions, however, need not serve the same purpose. Two Square rollouts illustrate how ExRL decides when to continue with a longer chunk. In Figure 9(b), it repeatedly truncates unsuitable predictions with little physical motion, then accepts a chunk that predicts a useful grasp-and-lift motion. Here, frequent replanning provides new candidate motions from nearly the same state. In Figure 9(c), short executions instead change the state through small corrections, bringing the nut closer to the peg before ExRL switches to longer execution. The distinction is between waiting for a useful prediction and moving into a state from which a longer prediction becomes useful. Both behaviors depend on the current state and the proposed chunk, rather than a fixed preference for short execution.

Figure 17 in the appendix illustrates how this balance unfolds across four real-world tasks. Further analysis shows that shuffling the same execution lengths across states and chunks reduces success (Appendix D-B). It also suggests a complementary reason to preserve longer execution: under feature aliasing, locally similar policy features can repeatedly produce similar first actions, so frequent replanning may interrupt useful progression through a chunk (Appendix D-C).

VI Conclusion

We introduced ExRL, which shifts online adaptation of long-chunk policies from action generation to execution-length control. Conditioning this scalar decision on the state and predicted chunk provides substantial behavioral flexibility, while keeping optimization low-dimensional as chunk size grows. Across simulation and real-world tasks, ExRL enables sample-efficient improvement of diverse frozen policies, often surpassing their best fixed execution length. Online imitation learning and offline demonstrations further extend these gains and support continued base-policy improvement during RL. These findings show that learning how to execute a policy’s predictions can unlock capabilities already present in the policy, making execution length a practical interface for adapting long-chunk robot policies with limited online interaction.

VII Limitations

Our real-world experiments keep the base policy frozen and do not yet incorporate online BC. Performance therefore remains constrained by the actions the base policy can propose, and several tasks still fall short of 100%100\% success. Extending online BC to these experiments may help address the remaining failures. We also adapt each task separately and have not evaluated joint multi-task adaptation or generalization to unseen tasks. Recent work demonstrates that sufficiently diverse multi-task experience and value-based RL can improve performance on unseen scenes and objects in simulation [29]; whether execution-length adaptation offers similar benefits remains open. Finally, we have not tested ExRL together with asynchronous inference methods such as real-time chunking (RTC) [10]. Understanding how adaptive replanning interacts with overlapping inference and execution is an important direction for extending ExRL to latency-sensitive deployments.

Appendix A Experimental Details

A-A Simulation Tasks and Demonstrations

Figure 10 illustrates the simulation tasks. Robomimic uses state observations comprising robot proprioception and object states, with control at 2020 Hz. Lift requires lifting a cube, Can requires placing a can in a bin, and Square requires fitting a nut onto a peg. Tool Hang involves assembling a frame and hanging a tool on it, while Transport requires two arms to transfer an object between bins. We train the base policies on 300300 Multi-Human (MH) demonstrations per task for Lift, Can, Square, and Transport, and on 200200 Proficient-Human (PH) demonstrations for Tool Hang [41].

Adroit uses state observations and controls a dexterous hand at 100100 Hz. Its four tasks require opening a door, driving a nail with a hammer, reorienting a pen, and relocating a ball to a target. The DP base policies are trained on the D4RL [19] expert-v2 datasets, containing 5,0005{,}000 trajectories each for Door, Hammer, and Relocate, and 4,9584{,}958 for Pen.

LIBERO uses image observations, proprioception, and a language instruction. We use the LIBERO-90 task “pick up the cream cheese and put it in the tray,” which runs at 2020 Hz and provides 5050 human demonstrations [38]. These demonstrations are used for task-specific fine-tuning of the generalist base policies described below.

Across all three benchmarks, ExRL uses a sparse reward of −1-1 at each primitive timestep before success and 00 upon success, when the episode terminates. Success is determined by the benchmark’s task-specific success condition.

A-B Policy Architectures and Pretraining

DP and ACT. Both policies condition on the current state and predict an HH-step action chunk. On Robomimic, DP uses a residual MLP denoiser with three hidden layers. The hidden width is 512512 for Lift and Can, 10241024 for Square, 20482048 for Tool Hang, and 40964096 for Transport. On Adroit, DP uses a temporal 1D U-Net with channel widths (128,256,512)(128,256,512) and a 128128-dimensional diffusion-step embedding. All DP models use 100100 diffusion steps during training; inference uses 55 DDIM steps on Lift and Adroit and 2020 on the other Robomimic tasks.

ACT uses a transformer encoder–decoder to predict the action chunk from state inputs. For Lift, Can, and Square, it has a hidden dimension of 512512, 88 attention heads, 44 encoder layers, 11 decoder layer, and a feedforward dimension of 32003200. For Tool Hang and Transport, these values are 768768, 1212, 66, 11, and 51205120, respectively. We train ACT without the variational latent encoder and execute its predicted chunks without temporal ensembling.

Table II reports the training epochs of the Robomimic base-policy checkpoints. For Adroit, we use DP checkpoints at epoch 22 for Door, Hammer, and Pen, and epoch 1010 for Relocate, with 10001000 gradient updates per epoch and a batch size of 10241024.

Generalist base policies. On LIBERO, we use the released π0\pi_{0} LIBERO checkpoint and task-specific checkpoints of π0.5\pi_{0.5}, π0\pi_{0}-FAST, and Cosmos-Policy after 5050, 10,00010{,}000, and 15001500 fine-tuning updates, respectively. All receive 224×224224\times 224 external-camera and wrist-camera images, proprioception, and the task instruction, and predict chunks of length H=50H=50.

ExRL on image observations. On LIBERO, ExRL encodes a 64×6464\times 64 external-camera image using four 3232-channel convolutional layers with 3×33\times 3 kernels, ReLU activations, and strides (2,1,1,1)(2,1,1,1). A fully connected layer projects the flattened features to a 5050-dimensional tanh bottleneck, which is concatenated with proprioception and the flattened predicted chunk. Ten 512×3512\times 3 MLP critic heads share the encoder and output values for each execution length. The SAC actor uses its own encoder and MLP of the same dimensions, with a categorical output. Random crops and color jitter augment images during RL updates.

A-C Action-Chunk Length Study

The left panel of Figure  examines how action-chunk length affects online adaptation. For convenience, we construct policies with different chunk sizes by exposing only the first L∈{2,4,8,16,25,50}L\in\{2,4,8,16,25,50\} actions of one pretrained DP checkpoint with H=50H=50 on Tool Hang. Each truncated policy presents the same black-box interface to the baseline RL policies as a base policy with chunk size LL: actions beyond the prefix are neither executed nor visible to their actors or critics. ResFiT and DICE-RL learn residual corrections only for the exposed LL actions, whereas ExRL-SAC selects an execution length k≤Lk\leq L from the exposed prefix.

For DSRL, we also restrict the learnable latent space to the prefix. Its actor outputs an L×daL\times d_{a} noise tensor, where da=7d_{a}=7 is the primitive action dimension. Inside the base-policy wrapper, the remaining (H−L)×da(H-L)\times d_{a} noise entries are independently sampled from a clipped Gaussian. The original diffusion policy then decodes the complete HH-step chunk, but the wrapper returns only the first LL actions. The action critic receives only this action prefix, and the noise critic receives only the actor’s LL-step noise; neither sees the hidden suffix. The pretrained diffusion model remains unchanged, while DSRL’s learned control dimension scales with LL. All variants use 2020 DDIM steps and a task horizon of 800800 primitive steps. We report three-seed means and 95%95\% confidence intervals.

The frozen DP on Tool Hang is itself less successful when executing long prefixes (Figure 16). To separate the effect of chunk length on RL adaptation from differences in base-policy performance, we additionally compare DSRL on Can, where DP has similar success rates across prefixes. As shown in Figure 11, DSRL quickly reaches near-perfect success with prefixes of 22–1616 actions, but learns substantially more slowly with 3232 and 5050 actions. The sample-efficiency gap thus persists even when the base policy performs similarly at different prefix lengths.

A-D Shared Hyperparameters

Most settings of ExRL are shared across tasks and base policies. Table III gives the defaults for ExRL-Q and ExRL-SAC, and Table IV lists the main task-specific changes. The same RL settings apply when Online BC is enabled.

Default episode horizons are 300300 for Lift and Can, 400400 for Square, 800800 for Tool Hang and Transport, 200200 for Adroit, and 250250 for LIBERO. Base-policy architectures and the LIBERO image encoder are described in Appendix A-B.

A-E Online BC and Demonstration Augmentation

Table V summarizes the default base-policy update settings. Successful trajectories are sampled uniformly over episodes, and BC starts once enough successful experience is available. For DP and ACT, we add a teacher constraint to the online BC loss using a frozen copy of the initial base policy. DP minimizes the mean squared difference between student and teacher noise predictions at identical observations, noisy chunks, and diffusion timesteps; ACT matches their inference-time action chunks at identical observations. The teacher stays fixed throughout RL, limiting drift from pretrained behavior as the student learns from successful online trajectories.

DP Tool Hang delays BC until 200200k environment steps. ACT uses a gradient-norm limit of 1010.

Demonstration augmentation. The default demonstration fraction in each BC batch is 0.50.5, and the frozen-teacher constraint is disabled. The number of BC updates per RL update decreases linearly from 55 to 11 over the first 600600k environment steps after BC begins, and remains at 11 thereafter.

Demonstrations in RL replay. For the Can comparison in Figure 7, the critic batch contains 20%20\% relabeled demonstration transitions and 80%80\% online transitions. The demonstration buffer holds up to 2.52.5M transitions, separately from the online replay.

A-F Baseline Implementations and Settings

We adapt the released baselines to our policy backbones and chunk sizes. Table VI summarizes hyperparameter selection; below, we describe changes to their policy interfaces and learning procedures.

DSRL. The released Robomimic configurations of Wagenmaker et al. [59] typically use chunks of 44 or 88 actions. We connect the official learner to our DP checkpoints and extend its latent action space to HH-step chunks. The diffusion sampler and normalization follow each checkpoint. We consider both DSRL-NA and DSRL-SAC during tuning. For example, the selected DP Transport and Tool Hang configurations use DSRL-SAC, a latent-noise bound of 0.750.75, and a learning rate of 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, with network widths of 20482048 and 512512, respectively. The restricted latent interface used in the prefix study is described in Appendix A-C.

Policy Decorator. We port the residual SAC learner of Yuan et al. [67] to our training framework while retaining bounded residual actions and progressive exploration. The residual has the same shape as the executed action chunk, and the actor conditions on both the observation and the base chunk, using the observation-plus-base-action option of the official code instead of its observation-only default. For DP with H=50H=50, the selected residual scales are 0.10.1, 0.150.15, 0.050.05, 0.020.02, and 0.020.02 on Lift, Can, Square, Tool Hang, and Transport, respectively. The two long-horizon tasks also use smaller entropy coefficients.

PA-RL. We implement Mark et al. [42] in our PyTorch framework, replacing its original base-policy interface with our DP and ACT models. Action optimization operates on complete chunks, and distillation uses the corresponding native training objective: denoising for DP and action reconstruction for ACT. We retain the official distributional critic ensemble and Cal-QL regularization, with 1010 critics, 22-critic target subsampling, and regularization coefficient 0.0050.005. Our main changes concern the interaction between critic learning, action optimization, and policy distillation. We first warm up the critic, then collect experience with optimized actions and periodically distill them into the base policy. For DP, we sample 3232 candidates and retain 1010 for optimization. ACT retains its deterministic inference, so repeated base candidates coincide; local optimization and the inclusion of replay actions provide the action-improvement step. Local search uses 1010–2020 gradient steps, with its step size and the distillation schedule tuned by task. On DP Lift, distillation uses globally selected candidates without local refinement, whereas rollout actions still receive local optimization. Lift, Can, and Square use online replay only. The H=50H=50 Transport and Tool Hang runs additionally mix equal proportions of offline demonstrations and online experience, following the official mixed-data recipe. Reported performance evaluates the optimized-action policy.

ResFiT. We extend the primitive-action residual formulation of Ankile et al. [3] to complete action chunks: the residual actor receives the state and base chunk, and the critic evaluates the composed chunk. Replay stores one transition per executed chunk, with accumulated discounted rewards and a bootstrap discount determined by its actual duration. We retain the TD3-style updates, 1010-critic ensemble, bounded residuals, and equal mixing of demonstration and online data. After searching on DP Square, we reuse actor/critic learning rates of 5×10−65\times 10^{-6}/10−410^{-4}, residual scale 0.10.1, exploration/target noise standard deviations of 0.0250.025/0.010.01, and target update rate 0.010.01. Each collected chunk transition receives one critic update and one actor update every four critic updates. We use one-chunk TD targets instead of the released primitive-step multi-step targets. Network width and discount remain task-specific. The same learner is used with ACT and Adroit; for LIBERO, we add image encoders and connect it to each policy’s native observation and action transforms.

OGPO. The released implementation of Patil et al. [47] uses flow-matching policies in JAX. To fine-tune our pretrained DP models directly, we implement its learning objectives in PyTorch and construct stochastic denoising trajectories around the DP’s DDIM transitions. We retain OGPO’s clipped likelihood-ratio objective and conservative group advantages, evaluating old and current likelihoods on the same denoising trajectory. We replace flow-matching regularization with the DP denoising loss on successful online experience. The standard runs use 3232 samples per advantage group and best-of-88 action selection during collection; evaluation samples a single trajectory from the target policy. We use lower update frequencies than the released configuration, with task-specific schedules for parallel collection and long chunks.

DICE-RL. We adapt Sun and Song [56] to our frozen DP and ACT policies while retaining its noise-conditioned residual, critic-guided candidate selection, and selective behavior regularization. For DP, the same noise conditions the base policy and residual actor. For ACT, the base chunk uses its standard deterministic inference, while noise conditions only the residual actor. We use the paper’s Can settings: 1010 critics, 1616 rollout/actor candidates, 44 target candidates, behavior-regularization weight 5050, and an offline replay fraction that decreases from 0.70.7 to 0.10.1 over 160160k environment steps. Relative to the released Can configuration, we enable the paper’s candidate-level Q filter and use constant learning rates of 10−410^{-4}. Demonstrations come from the datasets used for our base policies. Our replay stores non-overlapping chunk transitions, replacing the release’s overlapping action windows; three-step TD targets therefore span three chunk decisions, with rewards summed within each chunk and discounting applied between decisions. The RL batch size is 256256. Robomimic uses 2.52.5 critic updates per collected chunk transition, and Adroit uses one; the actor and target networks update half as frequently.

AAC. We adapt the released inference-time AAC selector [36] to each policy’s native chunk size. Robomimic and LIBERO use 2020 candidate chunks and the original entropy-increase rule with its motion constraint. On bimanual Transport, we sum the two arms’ entropies and average their motion measures. Adroit uses an entropy-only adaptation over joint actions with 6464 candidates, since the original Cartesian motion constraint does not apply. For π0\pi_{0}-FAST, auxiliary candidates use token sampling at temperature 11 to estimate entropy, while the executed candidate retains greedy decoding. In every case, AAC selects a prefix without averaging or re-ranking the candidate actions.

Other non-RL baselines. Random-kk samples uniformly from {1,…,H}\{1,\ldots,H\} at each query, and optimal fixed-kk reports the best fixed execution length from a sweep. Online BC executes full chunks and learns only from successful online trajectories, using the imitation objective and teacher constraint described in Appendix A-E, without RL updates or a learned execution-length policy.

A-G Details of Real-World Experiment

All real-world experiments use an AgileX Piper arm controlled at 2020 Hz. Each task uses a separate π0.5\pi_{0.5} base policy fine-tuned on human demonstrations. The policy receives third-person and wrist RGB views together with proprioceptive state, and predicts H=50H=50 actions. ExRL-Q keeps this policy frozen and selects the execution length using the mean of ten critics. Table VII summarizes the training settings.

Tasks and interaction. Our initial experiments study power insertion and parts organization (Figure 12). Insertion requires placing a charger plug into a power strip; organization requires placing four parts into separate compartments and closing the lid, giving five progress stages. We later extend the evaluation to stacking one cube on another and folding a T-shirt through three successive stages. During RL, the operator marks task or stage completion without providing action corrections or teleoperation.

Accounting for the cost of replanning. The initial insertion and organization experiments revealed a practical distinction between learning in fewer robot actions and completing a rollout quickly. Early in RL, the adapter often favored short execution lengths, requiring frequent queries to the large base policy and slowing each rollout. The original rewards did not directly penalize these inference pauses: insertion received −1-1 per primitive timestep before success and 00 at success, while organization received +1+1 for each completed stage and zero otherwise.

This observation motivated the elapsed-time objective used in our later stacking and folding experiments. Both the reward and discount now account for physical time, including inference within a rollout, so the adapter must balance the benefit of replanning against its time cost. For a decision lasting Δ\Delta seconds, the bootstrap discount is γΔ/0.05\gamma^{\Delta/0.05}, and the reward accumulates a discounted cost over the same interval. Stacking incurs unit cost per 5050-ms reference interval until success; folding weights this cost by the number of unfinished stages. The latter rewards both stage completion and timely progress through the remaining fold. Successful rollouts terminate, while ordinary time limits retain bootstrapping.

Policy preparation and training. The stacking and folding base policies are fine-tuned for 900900 and 10,00010{,}000 gradient steps, respectively, with folding updating the action expert. Stacking uses a D455 third-person camera and a D405 wrist camera; folding uses two D405 cameras. Folding views are cropped to 360×360360\times 360 before base-policy preprocessing and resized to 128×128128\times 128 for the critic. All tasks use critic learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, CQL weight 0.30.3, and two sampled target critics. We initialize the critic from warmup data before online adaptation; stacking and folding collect at least 256256 and 512512 transitions, respectively. Demonstration counts, update schedules, and rollout limits are given in Table VII.

Learning curves and evaluation. Figure  shows an EMA with coefficient 0.20.2, initialized at zero and updated after each rollout, including warmup. The outcome is binary success for stacking, folding, and insertion, and the fraction of completed stages for organization. For stacking and folding, the horizontal axis sums physical rollout time, including inference pauses but excluding resets, learner updates, and waiting between rollouts. The curves cover 10.0710.07 and 84.0684.06 minutes, respectively; insertion and organization use episode counts. Final evaluations are reported separately in Table I.

Appendix B On-Policy versus Off-Policy Adaptation

To examine how the choice of RL algorithm affects sample efficiency, we compare ExRL-Q with a PPO execution-length adapter, motivated by the PPO-based approach of Zhao et al. [71]. Both adapters use the same frozen DP checkpoint on Can, with chunk size H=50H=50, the same state and action-chunk inputs, and the same execution-length choices.

As shown in Figure 14, ExRL-Q reaches over 90%90\% success within approximately 33M environment steps, while PPO remains below 40%40\% after approximately 4040M steps. Curves average success over the most recent 200200 training episodes; the horizontal axis counts primitive environment steps. This substantial gap supports the use of off-policy learning for sample-efficient execution-length adaptation.

Appendix C Evolution of Learned Execution Lengths

Figure 15 examines how execution-length strategies develop during online adaptation. Alongside the mean execution length, we plot the categorical policy entropy averaged over training minibatches, which measures how concentrated the adapter’s decisions are for a given state and predicted chunk. Across tasks and base policies, the learned mean remains well below the full chunk size, but its evolution differs substantially. All four LIBERO policies rapidly settle at approximately 33–55 actions, whereas ACT on Square gradually favors longer execution, reaching about 1414 actions with H=50H=50 and 1111 with H=32H=32. Adroit Pen exhibits a similar increase.

Policy entropy further distinguishes these strategies. On ACT Square and Adroit Pen, increasing execution length accompanies decreasing entropy: the adapter becomes more decisive while allowing longer motions. In contrast, the LIBERO policies retain nonzero entropy after their mean execution lengths stabilize, so frequent replanning does not require deterministic length selection. The same adapter can therefore learn sustained frequent replanning or an increasing preference for longer motions, depending on the task and base policy.

Appendix D Additional Execution-Length Analysis

The behaviors in Section V-F suggest that ExRL benefits from choosing when to seek a new prediction and when to continue an existing one. Here we examine this interpretation beyond the main-text examples. We first establish that the execution patterns recur across tasks, then separate the effect of choosing suitable lengths from choosing them at suitable moments. Finally, we examine why frequent replanning can sometimes interrupt progress. The Robomimic analyses use frozen base policies with H=32H=32; the real-world examples use H=50H=50.

D-A Execution Patterns across Tasks

The tendency to shorten execution near interaction is consistent across tasks and random seeds. Figure 9(a) compares free motion with the approach to an object or insertion target, using the same trajectories for both phases. ExRL selects shorter lengths near interaction in all nine simulation task–seed pairs as well as on the real robot. This pattern persists when the distance threshold is changed from 88 cm to 66 or 1010 cm, suggesting that it reflects a recurring behavioral preference rather than a particular choice of phase boundary.

The real-world examples in Figure 17 show how this preference fits into a complete behavior. Stacking and folding use short adjustments around grasping before continuing with longer motions, while insertion concentrates replanning near contact. Parts organization, by contrast, sustains relatively long executions across much of its pick-and-place sequence. Repeated object interactions therefore do not necessarily require uniformly short execution: the appropriate length also depends on how effectively the predicted chunk carries the task forward.

For the phase comparison, we collect 5050 rollouts per simulation task and seed, and 2525 real insertion rollouts. We retain trajectories that reach interaction and contain both phases: 8686 for Lift, 145145 for Can, 121121 for Square, and 2121 for insertion. Queries before the first grasp or insertion are split by their starting distance to the object or target. We average selected lengths within each phase and then across trajectories; confidence intervals bootstrap trajectories.

D-B Matching Lengths to States and Chunks

A favorable mixture of short and long executions might explain some of ExRL’s gains even without adapting to the current situation. We isolate this possibility on Square by keeping the selected lengths unchanged but shuffling their assignment across environments at each synchronized query. The control receives exactly the same multiset of lengths as ExRL-Q, while losing the correspondence between each length and the state–chunk pair for which it was chosen.

This reassignment reduces success by 3838–5858 percentage points across DP and ACT (Table VIII). The benefit therefore lies not only in which lengths are used, but in when they are used. This result supports the interpretation of the main-text examples: short corrections, rejection of unsuitable chunks, and longer execution are useful when matched to the current state and prediction.

We use three independently trained ExRL-Q checkpoints per base policy. Paired rollouts share the initial state, initial chunk, and policy-inference randomness; confidence intervals resample checkpoint–environment-slot clusters.

D-C Feature Aliasing and Repeated Replanning

Short executions help when a new prediction provides a useful correction or alternative motion. But a new prediction can also restart the same behavior. Each query returns to the first action of a newly predicted chunk; if successive states produce similar policy inputs or internal features, these first actions may remain nearly unchanged. We refer to this local ambiguity as feature aliasing. In such situations, continuing through an existing chunk can preserve a progression that repeated replanning fails to recover.

This connection appears across both policy architectures. Over 3232-action replanning windows from 7272 states, smaller feature changes tend to accompany smaller changes in the newly predicted first arm action. The association is positive for DP and ACT on each of Lift, Can, and Square (Figure 18(a)), with overall Spearman correlation ρ=0.374\rho=0.374 (95%95\% CI [0.237,0.494][0.237,0.494]). A shorter, 1616-action window gives a similar correlation of 0.3830.383.

Physical motion alone need not break this repetition. Figure 18(b) compares two continuations from the same ACT Square state and initial chunk. In the shaded interval, replanning after every action moves the end effector by 19.419.4 mm, yet successive arm commands change by only 3.6%3.6\% as much as those along the original chunk. The robot moves, but the repeated predictions do not recover the later actions already available in that chunk. This example helps explain why allowing a useful prediction to unfold can be beneficial even when fresh observations are available.

Related analysis by Lazzati et al. [32] shows that conditioning on past observations can represent non-Markovian demonstrator behavior and mitigate compounding error, with these benefits also obtainable through delayed policies. Our observations provide a complementary perspective: while current features remain locally ambiguous, continuing a chunk may preserve behavioral progression that newly predicted first actions fail to provide.

Preserving this progression still requires choosing how long to continue. Table IX compares three continuations from the same selected ACT Square states: persistent one-action replanning, one full chunk followed by ExRL-Q, and ExRL-Q throughout. The adaptive strategy completes a case in which both alternatives fail. These diagnostic examples support a balance between obtaining new predictions when they help and retaining an existing prediction while it remains useful.

Measurement details. The ACT feature is the first decoder token; for DP, which has no learned observation encoder, we use the normalized conditioning input. We measure feature changes by normalized ℓ2\ell_{2} distance and arm-action changes by ℓ2\ell_{2} distance excluding the gripper. Window-level correlations are combined in Fisher-zz space, with equal weight across episodes and model–task pairs at the corresponding aggregation levels; confidence intervals resample episodes. The paired example uses the same initial state and chunk for both branches, and the three continuation states were selected before observing their outcomes.

Appendix E Execution-Length Control as an Induced SMDP

In this section, we formalize the connection between ExRL and semi-Markov decision processes (SMDPs) [58]. Recall that the underlying environment is a primitive-time MDP ℳ=(𝒮,𝒜,P,r,ρ0,γ)\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r,\rho_{0},\gamma), where each primitive action advances the environment by one timestep. ExRL does not change this environment. Instead, by freezing an action-chunked policy πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} and learning only how many actions from each predicted chunk to execute, ExRL induces a higher-level decision process over execution-length decisions.

Let 𝐚=at:t+H\mathbf{a}=a_{t:t+H} denote an action chunk sampled from the frozen base policy at state ss, i.e., 𝐚∼πbase(⋅∣s)\mathbf{a}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(\,\cdot\,\mid s). The high-level decision state is the pair

x=(s,𝐚)∈𝒳:=𝒮×𝒜H,x=(s,\mathbf{a})\in\mathcal{X}:=\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}^{H},

and the high-level action is the execution length k∈𝒦={1,…,H}k\in\mathcal{K}=\{1,\ldots,H\}. Thus, ExRL induces an SMDP

ℳex=(𝒳,𝒦,Pex,rex,Fex,ρex,γ),\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{ex}}=(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{K},P_{\mathrm{ex}},r_{\mathrm{ex}},F_{\mathrm{ex}},\rho_{\mathrm{ex}},\gamma),

where 𝒳\mathcal{X} is the decision-state space, 𝒦\mathcal{K} is the execution-length action space, Pex:𝒳×𝒦→Δ⁡(𝒳)P_{\mathrm{ex}}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{K}\rightarrow\Delta(\mathcal{X}) is the transition kernel over execution-level decision states, rex:𝒳×𝒦→ℝr_{\mathrm{ex}}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{K}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is the reward function for one execution-length decision, Fex:𝒳×𝒦→Δ⁡(ℕ)F_{\mathrm{ex}}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{K}\rightarrow\Delta(\mathbb{N}) is the duration distribution over primitive timesteps, ρex∈Δ⁡(𝒳)\rho_{\mathrm{ex}}\in\Delta(\mathcal{X}) is the initial decision-state distribution, and γ\gamma is the primitive-time discount factor inherited from the underlying MDP.

The initial decision-state distribution is induced by the environment initial state distribution and the frozen base policy:

s0∼ρ0,𝐚0∼πbase(⋅∣s0),x0=(s0,𝐚0)∼ρex.\begin{gathered}s_{0}\sim\rho_{0},\qquad\mathbf{a}_{0}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(\,\cdot\,\mid s_{0}),\\ x_{0}=(s_{0},\mathbf{a}_{0})\sim\rho_{\mathrm{ex}}.\end{gathered}

Given a decision state x=(st,𝐚t)x=(s_{t},\mathbf{a}_{t}) and an execution length ktk_{t}, the environment executes the prefix of the chunk for ktk_{t} primitive timesteps:

at,at+1,…,at+kt−1.a_{t},a_{t+1},\ldots,a_{t+k_{t}-1}.

This produces a trajectory segment (st,at,rt,…,st+kt)(s_{t},a_{t},r_{t},\ldots,s_{t+k_{t}}) under the primitive dynamics PP. The reward of the high-level decision is the discounted reward accumulated along this segment,

rex(x,kt)=𝔼[∑i=0kt−1γir(st+i,at+i)|x,kt].r_{\mathrm{ex}}(x,k_{t})=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=0}^{k_{t}-1}\gamma^{i}r(s_{t+i},a_{t+i})\,\middle|\,x,k_{t}\right].

After the prefix execution ends, the base policy is queried again at the new state st+kts_{t+k_{t}} to produce the next chunk 𝐚′∼πbase(⋅∣st+kt)\mathbf{a}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(\,\cdot\,\mid s_{t+k_{t}}). Therefore, the next high-level decision state is

x′=(st+kt,𝐚′).x^{\prime}=(s_{t+k_{t}},\mathbf{a}^{\prime}).

Let KK denote the realized duration of executing length ktk_{t}. Starting from x=(st,𝐚t)x=(s_{t},\mathbf{a}_{t}), the primitive dynamics generate states st+1,…,st+Ks_{t+1},\ldots,s_{t+K} by executing the prefix of 𝐚t\mathbf{a}_{t} until either ktk_{t} actions have been executed or the episode terminates. The duration distribution is

Fex​(K∣x,kt)\displaystyle F_{\mathrm{ex}}(K\mid x,k_{t})
=Pr(K​ primitive timesteps elapsebefore the next decision|x,kt).\displaystyle=\Pr\!\left(\begin{gathered}K\text{ primitive timesteps elapse}\\ \text{before the next decision}\end{gathered}\,\middle|\,x,k_{t}\right).

In the non-terminal case, Fex(K∣x,kt)=𝟙{K=kt}F_{\mathrm{ex}}(K\mid x,k_{t})=\mathbbm{1}\{K=k_{t}\}; if the episode terminates early, then K<ktK<k_{t} is the actual number of primitive steps executed and no bootstrap term is used.

The transition kernel over decision states is

Pex​(x′∣x,kt)\displaystyle P_{\mathrm{ex}}(x^{\prime}\mid x,k_{t})
=Pr(st+K=s′,𝐚′∼πbase(⋅∣s′)∣x,kt),\displaystyle=\Pr\!\left(s_{t+K}=s^{\prime},\;\mathbf{a}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(\,\cdot\,\mid s^{\prime})\mid x,k_{t}\right),
x′=(s′,𝐚′).\displaystyle x^{\prime}=(s^{\prime},\mathbf{a}^{\prime}).

That is, PexP_{\mathrm{ex}} is induced by first rolling out the primitive dynamics under the selected prefix, and then querying the frozen base policy at the resulting state to form the next decision state.

For an execution-length policy πex​(k∣x)\pi_{\mathrm{ex}}(k\mid x), the SMDP Bellman equation is

Qπex(x,k)=𝔼[R+γKVπex(x′)|x,k],Q^{\pi_{\mathrm{ex}}}(x,k)=\mathbb{E}\left[R+\gamma^{K}V^{\pi_{\mathrm{ex}}}(x^{\prime})\,\middle|\,x,k\right],

where

R=∑i=0K−1γi​r​(st+i,at+i),Vπex(x′)=𝔼k′∼πex(⋅∣x′)[Qπex(x′,k′)],\begin{gathered}R=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}\gamma^{i}r(s_{t+i},a_{t+i}),\\ V^{\pi_{\mathrm{ex}}}(x^{\prime})=\mathbb{E}_{k^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ex}}(\cdot\mid x^{\prime})}\left[Q^{\pi_{\mathrm{ex}}}(x^{\prime},k^{\prime})\right],\end{gathered}

and KK is the realized duration of the high-level execution-length decision. When the episode does not terminate during the prefix execution, K=kK=k.

This recovers the duration-aware TD target used in ExRL. Writing x=(st,at:t+H)x=(s_{t},a_{t:t+H}), x′=(s′,a′)x^{\prime}=(s^{\prime},a^{\prime}), and K=ktK=k_{t}, the target becomes

yt=∑i=0kt−1γi​r​(st+i,at+i)+γkt​V​(s′,a′),y_{t}=\sum_{i=0}^{k_{t}-1}\gamma^{i}r(s_{t+i},a_{t+i})+\gamma^{k_{t}}V(s^{\prime},a^{\prime}),

where VV is instantiated by the particular RL algorithm, such as a greedy value for ExRL-Q or a soft value for ExRL-SAC. Thus, the only difference from a standard one-step Bellman backup is that the selected high-level action ktk_{t} determines the duration of the transition. As a result, ktk_{t} affects not only the accumulated reward and next decision state, but also the bootstrap discount through the factor γkt\gamma^{k_{t}}.
